title: What is known about 1RB1LC_1RC0RF_1RD0LB_1RE0LD_1LF---_0RA1LA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LC_1RC0RF_1RD0LB_1RE0LD_1LF---_0RA1LA.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and it is a Collatz-like one. The run from blank tape is proved in Lean, with exact step counts, through the whole first level (more than 101543 steps) to the first configuration of the second level. Every reset at a short tail is a theorem for every n, and the list of short tails closes up after a third level: two classes halt, 29 classes loop forever, and the others start a new level or a new phase. Every level runs a prefix of one orbit of one digit map, f(10a + d) = 31a + K[d/2] from 22, and Lean proves the machine halts exactly when the walk halts where that orbit runs out of the 772-digit budget of level 2: about 2·10770 steps along it, with no closed form known. The orbit is the rational base 31/10 expansion of 22, whose digits re-encode every digit of the start (a theorem), and 108 exact steps of it look like random digits.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (E1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 62,434 cells have been visited and 38,014 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 7.07·10<sup>19,058</sup> steps (accelerated run, Quick_Sim)
claims.text: Shawn Ligocki's Quick_Sim.py (github.com/sligocki/busy-beaver, commit cc35611) with recursive rules (-r: a macro machine with a block size it picks itself and a back symbol, rules proved symbolically from repeated tape shapes, and rules whose proofs use earlier rules) runs 3,923,081 loops from blank tape without a halt, in 121 seconds of a 2-minute screen. That is more than 7.07·1019,058 machine steps. It is an outside program, run here without changes; it reported no rule that repeats forever, so it does not decide the machine.

claims.title: The turns at the left end, for every block length
claims.text: 0^inf (1100)^(n+1) C> 11 R and 0^inf 1 (1001)^(n+1) A> 1 R both reach 0^inf 1 (1001)^(n+1) 1001 B> R (16n+32 and 16n+33 steps): the head crosses the c block leftwards, bounces and crosses it back. From 0^inf A> 0 (1100)^(n+1) R it reaches 0^inf (1100)^(n+1) 1 B> R in 6n+7 steps. For all n and every tape R.

claims.title: A period, and a phase of periods, for every size
claims.text: 0^inf B> 0 0 1 (1100)^n (10110110)^(m+5) R reaches 0^inf B> 0 0 1 (1100)^(n+31) (10110110)^m R in 448n + 6952 steps, for all n, m and every tape R (it is never read); by induction, q periods take (n, m + 5q) to (n + 31q, m).

claims.title: An accelerated simulator, checked against the machine
claims.text: c/m7fast.c runs the machine and applies the period rule in one stroke wherever the tape has that form, with the exact step count. With VAL=11 it runs the plain machine beside it and compares the whole tape and state at 1,164 checkpoints (every jump and every record on the left in between) up to 5.9·1010 steps: no difference.

claims.title: The run to 4.5·10<sup>17</sup> steps

The reset of (6,799, 1), at step 373,111,704, writes the tail 10 (1110)^6805 1. No halt; the tape needed is then about 109 cells.

claims.title: The phase map, and 2,177 phases from (17, 0, 6805)
claims.text: phase on (n, r, t) is the reset followed by its periods (the map of py/m7map.py). phase_spec and phaseRun_spec: the machine follows it, k phases at a time, with the exact step counts, for every tape R beyond the tail; phaseRun_some: it applies for k phases whenever t ≥ 4k. Evaluated by the kernel from (17, 0, 6805): the first five phase ends and step counts are those of the run above, and after 2,177 phases (about 101543 steps) the map reaches r = 3, t = 0 with n of 772 digits, without a halt; phase 2,176 ends at r = 3, t = 3. With fewer words than a row reads the constructed tapes show other resets, which rebuild a tail of about n words followed by a new suffix (1001101011001): a second level of the same kind, beyond any simulation. That the run from blank tape reaches (17, 0, 6805) with the tail 10 (1110)^6805 1, and what the reset after phase 2,177 does, are proved too (next claim).

claims.title: From blank tape to the start of the second level
claims.text: Before the long tail exists the tail after the d block is 1001, and its resets are rules for every n: (n, 0) starts the new phase (10, ⌊n/2⌋ − 1) and (n, 2) the phase (10, ⌈n/2⌉ + 6), both keeping 1001; (n, 1) writes the long tail, (17, 0) with 10 (1110)^(n+6) 1. The first 7,106 steps (evaluated by the kernel on the list simulator) reach (10, 10) with the tail 1001; periods and these resets then give the phase ends (72, 0), (227, 0), (692, 2), (2,180, 2), (6,799, 1) and (17, 0, 6805) at step 374,475,636, exactly as measured. Level 1 (the phase map, previous claim) ends after 2,177 phases at (N, 3, 0) with the suffix 1; that reset reads the suffix and reaches (17, 0) with the tail 10 (1110)^(N+20) 1001101011001 in 440N + 9367 steps. So from blank tape the machine reaches, without halting, the first record of level 2, with N ≡ 63 (mod 100), 10771 ≤ N < 10772, after more than 101543 steps.

claims.title: A halting class on the second level, and the way into it
claims.text: From 0^inf B> 0 0 1 (1100)^(n+1) (10110110)^2 10 (1110)^2 1001101011001 0^inf the machine halts, for every n. The class is reachable from larger tails through the proved reset table: a phase end with six words 1110 left, r = 0 and n ≡ 0 or 9 (mod 10) resets to (10, ⌊(n+5)/2⌋) with two words left, and its periods end at r = 2: the machine halts. On the first-level tail (suffix 1) no class halts.

claims.title: Fourteen classes never halt
claims.text: The loop record 0^inf B> 0 0 1 (1100)^(n+1) 0 1 0^inf reaches the same record with five more words 1100 in 80n + 395 steps, so from it the machine runs for ever. Two classes of the tail 1001, six of the first-level tail and four of the second-level tail (and the loop record itself) reach it; for example r = 1 with the tail 101, seen for 3,000 rounds on 13 November, is now a theorem.
claims.where: loop5, loop_runs, s1_r1_t0_never_halts and the other *_never_halts, lean/NearEmpty.lean; the older measured tables runs/classes_tail1.txt, runs/classes_tail2.txt

claims.title: The third level: the short tails close up
claims.text: Some second-level resets leave a short tail that is not a nearly empty tail of a suffix: 1100 1011001, 10 1101001, or 1001101011001 right after the d block. The reset at each of them, for every r that occurs, and at every short tail those lead to, is a theorem for every n: 39 rules. Only nine further short tails come up, and then nothing new, so the list is closed. One new suffix appears, 1011001: from 1001101011001 right after the d block with r = 0 the machine builds a long tail of n + 3 words 1110 ending in 1011001, the third level, and all fourteen nearly empty tails of that suffix are among the 39. The ends are: a long tail of suffix 1, 1001101011001 or 1011001 (a new level 1, 2 or 3), the tail 1001 of level 0, the loop record (fifteen more classes that never halt), or a halt: 0^inf B> 0 0 1 (1100)^n (10110110)^2 10 1101001 0^inf halts for every n. A second-level phase end with r = 2, one word 1110 left and n ≡ 6 or 7 (mod 10) gets there through the periods, so it halts too. With the generic rows of the reset table, which hold for any suffix, every reset the machine can meet from these levels is now proved: the run is a walk through a finite table of proved transitions, driven by the numbers n, r and t.
claims.where: lean/Level3.lean (y0_r2_halts, s2_r2_t1_to_y_halts, s2_r0, *_never_halts, …), lean/Level3Rules.lean, both generated by lean/level3.py; the closure measured by py/closure_table.py (c/firstrec.c), output in runs/closure_table.txt

claims.title: Halting is a question about one map on numbers
claims.text: Every proved rule is put into one function on records (n, m, T), where T is a long tail of one of the three suffixes or one of the ten short tails. It applies the periods, the generic reset, or one of 72 rows for the nearly empty and short tails, and it ends in a halting class or in the loop record. Lean proves that the table covers every record the run can meet, and that each step is a real run of the machine. The machine halts from blank tape if and only if this walk, started at (17, 0) with 6805 words 1110 and the suffix 1, reaches a halting class. The walk is plain arithmetic, but level 2 alone takes about 10771 of its steps on numbers of about 10770 digits, so it cannot be followed to the end.

claims.title: Every level is a prefix of one orbit of one digit map
claims.text: On a long tail the walk of the table is the map f(10a + d) = 31a + K[d/2], K = 15, 27, 47, 35, 36, on one number x that stands for the phase end (10 + 31⌊x/10⌋, ⌊(x mod 10)/2⌋); one step of f uses 4, 5, 8, 3 or 2 words 1110 for r = 0, ..., 4, for every suffix. Every level starts at (17, 0), which after one phase is x = 22, so every level runs the same orbit 22, 89, 284, 915, ... and stops where its words run out. Level 1 (6801 words) stops after 1566 steps at r = 3 with no word left (by decide). The machine halts from blank tape if and only if the walk halts from the state where the orbit of 22 stops with the 772-digit budget of level 2.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>186095</sup> steps (region-memo accelerator)
claims.text: The region-memo accelerator tools/py/bbtools/regaccel.py ran with blocks of 8 cells, from blank tape for 1800 seconds and reached a step count of 186,096 digits (so at least 10186095) without a halt. With blocks of 4 cells the same engine stalls near 109: the words 10110110 of length 8 split into two different 4-cell blocks, so every run of them is broken up; with blocks of 8 they become one long run, and the first and second level of the counter are both visible on the tape ((11101110)^~10^771, the second-level tail of about 10771 words). It keeps the tape run-length coded and, for each stretch of tape from the left end, a macro (the run until the head first leaves that stretch) computed by a symbolic run of the machine with the long runs as variables; a macro is used only when the linear inequalities its symbolic run assumed hold, otherwise the stretch is run again by the same recursion. So the run is exact, step count included. Check: 7 configurations of this run (every time the head faced blank tape on the right, up to 2×109 steps) agree cell for cell with a direct run (tools/py/regcheck.py). This is a bounded run and says nothing about later steps.

claims.title: The digit map in closed form: a rational base 31/10 expansion whose digits re-encode the start
claims.text: The exact identity 10<sup>k</sup>x<sub>k</sub> + 31Σ31<sup>k−1−i</sup>10<sup>i</sup>d<sub>i</sub> = 31<sup>k</sup>x<sub>0</sub> + 10Σ31<sup>k−1−i</sup>10<sup>i</sup>K<sub>i</sub> writes the start 22 in the rational base 31/10, with the orbit's digits as its digits. For every k, the first k values of r depend only on the start mod 10<sup>k</sup>, and every list of k values occurs for some start below 10<sup>k</sup>: no finite pattern of the orbit rules out a halting row. The last bit of a state never matters; on x/2 the map is 31⌊y/10⌋ + G[y mod 10].

claims.title: The orbit of 22 followed exactly for 10<sup>8</sup> steps
claims.text: A divide-and-conquer run (GMP) follows the digit map for 10<sup>8</sup> steps in 6 minutes; the last state has 49,136,172 digits. All 5<sup>L</sup> blocks of r values occur for L ≤ 9, chi-square against uniform has |z| ≤ 2.03 at every block length, and the words used stay within 1.6 standard deviations of a random walk. Ending a level at 440,229 sampled steps, level 2 halts 5.44% of the time and a halt from the start of level 2 comes out at 6.2% when chained over levels: the 40,000-step figures stand. No structure that a closed form could use shows up.

claims.title: Where the real run stands
claims.text: The first level of the real run is proved (above) and ends at (N, 3, 0), N ≡ 63 (mod 100), a number of 772 digits; the second level starts with a tail of N + 20 words 1110 (proved). It then lasts about (N + 20)/2.5 phases of the proved phase map, about 10771, with n roughly tripling in each, and how it ends (one of the two halting classes, a loop, a return to the tail 1001 or a third level, all in the proved and closed table) depends on r, t and the parity or last digit of n at that moment, which nobody can compute. So the closed-set method does not apply: a halting class is reachable, and this is a Collatz-like question.

claims.title: How a level ends, measured on the real orbit
claims.text: Along the first 40,000 steps of the orbit of 22 each value of r comes up 19.7% to 20.2% of the time. Weighting every budget that stops between steps 2,000 and 40,000 alike, a level with the suffix 1001101011001 (level 2) ends in a proved loop 59.7% of the time, starts level 3 22.8%, level 1 7.6%, level 2 4.5%, and halts 5.4%. Chaining these odds over levels gives about a 6% chance that the machine ever halts. The last digits of an orbit are a one-to-one recoding of the start's digits (31 is invertible mod 10k), so no rule reading a bounded number of digits predicts the end, and no closed form for the orbit at step 2·10770 is known.
claims.where: python3 py/endgame.py 40000 (16 s; the rows are read from lean/Walk.lean by py/walksim.py)

claims.title: Available in Lean here as a cited axiom: DeepMind's halts-iff map
claims.text: deepmind_halts_iff states on this repository's definitions what DeepMind's compiled theorem proves: the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the orbit of their map next from start reaches none. The map is copied from their file unchanged, and running the copy and theirs for 120 steps gives the same states. It is an axiom: nothing in this repository proves it, and the translation from DeepMind's definitions (Mathlib's Turing machines) to ours is not checked by Lean. #print axioms names it in every theorem that uses it.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The only halting transition is E reading 1. It is proved that the machine halts exactly when the walk of the proved table halts from the point where the orbit of 22 under the digit map f(10a + d) = 31a + K[d/2] runs out of the 772-digit budget of level 2. That point is about 2·10<sup>770</sup> steps along the orbit; no closed form is known, and the real orbit's statistics suggest a proved loop is the likeliest end (about 6% for a halt).

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. This machine keeps two blocks of words side by side: one grows while the other shrinks, and when the second is used up the first is turned into it, about three times larger than last time.

facts.text: No halt in a region-memo run with 8-cell blocks (30 minutes).
One period trades five d words for 31 c words; proved in Lean for every size.
Followed exactly, jumping over the periods, without a halt.
Proved in Lean from blank tape: the whole first level, up to the first configuration of the second.
Every reset at a short tail, on all three levels, proved for every n: two classes halt, 29 never do, and the table closes.
Every level runs the same orbit 22, 89, 284, ... of f(10a + d) = 31a + K[d/2]; only its budget of words differs.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.561). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 62,434 cells (48,420 left of the start, 45 right), with a density of 1s of 0.609.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Two blocks of words
html:
Left of the start the tape reads

0^inf c^n J d^m 1 0 (1110)^r ...

with c = 1100, d = 10110110 and a short junction J. The head shuttles between the left end and J; the bounces at the left end are proved in Lean. J cycles through a few shapes, and over the cycle the c block gains about 6.2 words for each d word it eats.

sections.heading: When the d's run out
html:
A period of 84 trips to the left end trades five d's for 31 c's; Lean proves this for every size and whatever lies further right. When fewer than five d's are left the phase ends with a remainder r, and a reset follows. From step 3.7·108 on, the tail right of the d's is a run of t words 1110, and the resets follow an exact table, proved in Lean for every n:

A new phase starts with n = 10 and m′ d's and ends after ⌊m′/5⌋ periods. So n roughly triples from phase to phase while t shrinks by one to four words. The table reproduces every phase end of the run to 4.5·1017 steps; iterated on its own (a Lean theorem) it lasts 2,176 more phases, until t is almost used up, and then a different reset builds a much longer tail: the same structure one level up.

sections.heading: Two classes halt, 29 loop: all proved
html: A method that settled another holdout keeps the big counts free and follows only small remainders; it proves non-halting when no remainder class can halt. Here it finds the opposite. Leave the number n of words 1100 free and take every remainder r with fewer words 1110 left than the reset needs; Lean proves what happens for every n:

The run from blank tape is proved to that point, more than 101543 steps. The short tails that the resets leave close up: after the third level nothing new comes, so every reset the machine can meet is proved. From there the machine can halt, loop forever, go back to its start-up tail or start a new level, depending on a remainder after about 10771 phases in which n triples each time. That is the same kind of question as the Collatz problem, and no proof either way is in sight.

sections.heading: Every level runs the same orbit
html: On a long tail the proved table is, phase by phase, one map on one number. Write a phase end (n, r) as a single number x with n = 10 + 31⌊x/10⌋ and r = ⌊(x mod 10)/2⌋. Then the next phase end is

and that phase uses 4, 5, 8, 3 or 2 words 1110 of the tail (r = 1 and 2 are a reset that goes straight into an r = 0 reset, so one step of f is two phases there). Lean proves this from the walk of the table (digit_step, lean/DigitMap.lean). Every level starts at (17, 0) with T words; its first phase gives x = 22 with T − 4 words (level_start). So every level runs the same orbit 22, 89, 284, 915, … of f, and the only thing that differs is how many words it has: it stops at the first state whose phase needs more words than are left. Level 1 had 6,801 and stopped after 1,566 steps (level1_digit, by decide); level 2 has B = 10 + 31⌊X1/10⌋ + 16, a number of 772 digits. Lean proves the machine halts exactly when the walk halts from the state where the orbit stops with B words (halts_iff_level2_end).

Try budgets up to a few hundred thousand words; the orbit is exact (BigInt) and the last row is the proved row of the table that the end meets. The budget of level 2 has 772 digits, so its end is about 2·10770 steps along this orbit, on numbers of about 10770 digits.

The closed form there is. Three facts are proved for every number of steps (lean/DigitClosed.lean, kernel):

  • An exact identity. With di the last digit of xi and Ki its constant, 10kxk + 31Σi<k 31k−1−i10idi = 31kx0 + 10Σi<k 31k−1−i10iKi (orbit_identity). Divided by 31k, it writes the start 22 in the rational base 31/10, and the orbit's digits are the digits of that expansion. It is exact, but the last digit of xk is read off a sum over all the earlier digits, so it skips nothing.
  • The digits re-encode the start. The first k values of r depend only on the start mod 10k, and every list of k values occurs for some start below 10k (rlist_mod, rlist_onto; 31 is invertible mod 10k, inv31). Any finite pattern can be followed by anything, so no rule that watches a bounded window of the orbit can keep it out of a halting row.
  • One bit is spare. The last bit of a state never matters; on y = x/2 the map is 31⌊y/10⌋ + G[y mod 10] with G = 7, 13, 23, 17, 18, 23, 29, 39, 33, 33 (fd_half), a mod-10 map of slope 31/10 in which all ten digits count.

Nothing faster than following the orbit is known for expansions like this (it is Mahler’s 3/2 problem in another base, and the same kind of question as the Antihydra holdout). The budget fixes where level 2 ends only to within about 10385 steps of the orbit, and those steps are on numbers of about 10770 digits.

What the real orbit suggests. Because the high digits of a state ride along as a multiple of 31c (orb_split), the orbit can be followed exactly by divide and conquer: py/orbitfast.py does 108 steps in 6 minutes (the last state has 49,136,172 digits). Each r comes up 19.996% to 20.005% of the time, every one of the 59 = 1,953,125 blocks of nine r values occurs, the block counts pass a chi-square test against uniform at every length up to 9 (|z| ≤ 2.03), and the words used stay within 1.6 standard deviations of a random walk.
